title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook: Process, Runbooks, Postmortems, Rotations, Game Days, Status Page & Customer Comms
author: Jordan Patel
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines Redwood Inference's standard on-call and incident response practices: severity classification, triage process, runbook structure, postmortem expectations, on-call rotation rules, game-day exercises, and status page / customer communications templates. It is the canonical reference for on-call engineers, incident commanders (ICs), and stakeholders during incidents.

Scope:
- All production-facing services (hosted API, dedicated runtime, private deployments)
- Customer-impacting degradations, data plane outages, severe performance regressions, and security incidents (see security-and-compliance pages for handling PII / breaches)

Goals:
- Restore service as quickly and safely as possible
- Communicate clearly to internal and external stakeholders
- Capture root cause and action items to prevent recurrence

1) Incident classification and severity
Use the following severity rubric for initial triage. Update severity as more information becomes available.

| Severity | Definition | Response SLA | Escalation |
|---------|-----------|--------------|-----------|
| Sev 1 | Service down or >50% of customers affected; requests failing or responses unusable | Acknowledge: 5 min; Mitigation started: 15 min | Pager -> IC -> Eng leads -> Execs |
| Sev 2 | Major degradation (latency, errors) impacting many customers but partial service available | Acknowledge: 15 min; Mitigation: 60 min | Pager -> IC -> Service owner |
| Sev 3 | Functional impact to small subset or intermittent errors; non-urgent | Acknowledge: 1 business day | Ticket and triage during next business hours |

2) Incident lifecycle (high level)
1. Detection & Alerting: PagerDuty or monitoring alerts land with runbook link
2. Acknowledge & Triage: On-call acknowledges, reads runbook, and assesses severity
3. Assign IC & Roles: Appoint Incident Commander (IC), Communications lead, Subject Matter Experts (SMEs), and Scribe
4. Mitigation & Containment: Execute runbook play; apply mitigations to stop customer impact
5. Restore & Validate: Confirm service health and SLOs; iterate mitigations if needed
6. Communicate: Update internal channels (Slack #incidents) and external status page at standard intervals
7. Postmortem: Complete postmortem within 72 hours (draft) and publish within 7 days with action items

3) Roles & responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): Leads technical decisions, drives timeline, coordinates mitigations.
- Communications Lead: Owns external and internal updates, drafts status page entries.
- Scribe: Takes timeline notes and records decisions.
- SMEs / Service Owner: Executes runbook steps and implements fixes.
- Escalation (Engineering Lead / On-Call Manager): Decides cross-team resource allocation and exec notif.

Contact methods: primary = PagerDuty -> phone -> Slack -> email. Escalation timeouts: follow PagerDuty policy; IC can shortcut escalation for urgent resource needs.

4) Runbook structure & naming convention
- Filename convention: <team>-<service>-runbook-YYYYMMDD.md (stored in confluence and repo)
- Required sections in every runbook:
  - Summary & scope
  - Owners & contacts (PagerDuty schedule)
  - Detection & key metrics (alerts, dashboards, SLOs)
  - Impact indicators & severity mapping
  - Quick mitigation steps (Step 0..N) for initial containment
  - Deep-dive diagnostic commands and queries
  - Post-incident checklist & follow-ups
  - Last reviewed date and review cadence (quarterly)

Example quick mitigation for API 503 spike:
1) Verify error rate: `kubectl logs -l app=frontend-api --since=10m | jq .status | grep 503 | wc -l`
2) Check autoscaler events and pod restarts: `kubectl get hpa && kubectl describe deployment frontend-api`
3) If backend datastore is overloaded: switch traffic to read-only replica or scale replicas: `kubectl scale deploy/frontend-api --replicas=5`
4) Roll back recent config change if deploy in last 15 minutes: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/frontend-api`

Diagnostic commands (examples):
- Check GC / OOM: `dmesg | tail` and `kubectl describe pod`
- Check GPU failures: `nvidia-smi` and runtime logs at /var/log/runtime/*
- Trace request path: `curl -v https://api.redwood.ai/health` and check envoy/access logs

5) Escalation matrix (example)
- On-call engineer (10 min) -> Service owner (20 min) -> SRE lead (30 min) -> CTO (60 min for ongoing Sev 1)
- Cross-team pager: use #incidents-sre initial channel and create incident Slack channel `#incident-<YYMMDD>-<service>`

6) Postmortem template (must be filled for Sev 1/2; recommended for Sev 3)
- Title: [SEV] Service - Short summary
- Date / Timeline: chronological events with timestamps and actor initials
- Summary: one-paragraph impact and outcome
- Root Cause: concise cause (what broke and why)
- Contributing Factors: partial failures, monitoring blind spots, process gaps
- Mitigations & Immediate Fixes: what we did to restore
- Long-term Remediation: code / infra / process changes with owners and due dates
- Action items: list with owner, due date, status (open/closed)
- Lessons Learned & Preventive measures
- Severity justification and customer comms status

Postmortem deadlines: Draft within 72 hours; stakeholders review within 5 business days; publish internal + link on external status page summary within 10 business days (unless restricted).

7) On-call rotations & best practices
- Rotation length: 1 week for primary on-call; 2 weeks max for secondary (backup).
- Handover: 15-minute synchronous overlap on Monday; on-call must publish a handover note in the rotation doc and Slack thread.
- Buddying: new on-callers should buddy with an experienced on-caller for first rotation.
- Time off: book rotation swaps at least 72 hours in advance; emergency swaps require Eng Lead approval.
- Overrides: for holidays or exec travel, rotations can be extended but must be approved and documented.
- On-call expectations: monitor alerts, respond to pages within SLA, update runbooks after incidents, attend postmortems.

8) Game days (exercise program)
Objectives:
- Validate runbooks, tools, and communication flows
- Surface monitoring gaps and cross-team coordination issues
- Practice escalation and mitigation steps under time pressure

Game day cadence and checklist:
- Frequency: quarterly per major product team; critical infra teams monthly for high-risk components
- Pre-game prep: announce objectives, select IC & Communications Lead, prepare test scenarios, create a firewalled test org if customer impact risk exists
- During game day: run scenario, record timeline, keep communication cadence to mimic real incident
- Post-game: immediate <48h> short retro, 7-day detailed follow-up with action items tracked in Jira

Sample scenarios:
- Primary DB becomes read-only under load
- Model inference nodes OOM under long sequences
- Cross-region service degradation with automatic failover not triggering

9) Status page & customer communications templates
Standard cadence: initial acknowledgement (within 30 minutes for Sev 1), regular updates (every 30-60 minutes while active), resolution notice, and post-incident summary.

Template: Initial Acknowledgement (external)
- Subject: [Incident] <service> - Investigating - <short impact summary>
- Body: "We are aware of an issue affecting <service> causing <impact>. Our on-call team has been engaged and is investigating. We will provide updates every 30-60 minutes or as the situation changes. Reference: <status.redwood.ai/incidents/ID>"

Template: Internal Update (Slack)
- Timestamp | Severity | Summary | Actions taken | Next steps | Owner(s)
- Example: `10:12 UTC | SEV1 | API 503 spike for hosted customers | scaled frontend to 5 replicas, rollback attempted | continue to monitor errors & throttle non-critical jobs | IC: @jordan`

Template: Resolution Notice (external)
- Subject: [Resolved] <service> - <short summary>
- Body: "The issue affecting <service> has been resolved at <time>. Root cause: <summary>. Actions: <short immediate fixes>. We are preparing a post-incident report and will publish a summary within 10 days. If you continue to see problems, contact support@redwood.ai."

Template: Post-incident Summary (external short)
- Summary of impact, root cause, customer guidance, mitigation completed, and planned long-term fixes with timeline and contact for follow-up.

10) Metrics & SLO considerations during incident
- Key dashboards to check: error-rate (5m/1m), p50/p90/p99 latencies, request throughput, CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, and backend datastore metrics.
- Thresholds to consider escalation: p99 latency >2x baseline or error rate >3% for >5 minutes triggers a Sev 2 investigation; service unavailable for >5 minutes triggers Sev 1.

11) Documentation & review cadence
- Runbooks: reviewed quarterly or after any incident affecting the runbooked flow
- Postmortems: tracked to closure of action items in Jira; owners accountable for on-time completion
- Game days: retro notes fed to runbook updates and monitoring improvements

12) Templates & checklists (appendix)
- Incident start checklist: acknowledge -> create incident channel -> assign IC & scribe -> set status page -> run quick mitigation steps -> escalate if needed
- Incident close checklist: confirm restored -> monitor for 1-2 hours -> close incident channel and create postmortem ticket -> notify stakeholders and customers

Appendix: Helpful links and contacts
- PagerDuty schedules: /confluence/eng-sre/pagerduty-schedules
- Incident templates repo: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/templates
- SLO definitions: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets

If you are unsure during an incident: take a conservative approach (isolate traffic, remove risky changes, prioritize customer safety), escalate early, and communicate often. This playbook is the living source of truth; update your runbook after any practice or real incident to keep it accurate.
